why_use_this: Reach for this package when you need to find the input that minimizes (or, for `simplex_solve`, maximizes subject to linear constraints) a function -- fitting a model's parameters, finding a system's equilibrium, solving a resource-allocation problem. It covers three genuinely different problem shapes with different tools: unconstrained smooth optimization (gradient descent through Newton's method, picked by how much curvature information you're willing to supply), constrained optimization via the penalty method (turns constraints into an added cost term so an unconstrained solver can still be used), and linear programming via the simplex method (exact, for problems that are genuinely linear in both objective and constraints). If your problem is a nonlinear ROOT-finding problem (\( F(x)=0 \)) rather than a minimization problem, that's [vani-algebra](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-algebra)'s `algebra_newton_system` instead, even though the underlying Newton-step machinery looks similar. Every gradient-consuming function here also has a `_fd` (finite-difference) variant for when you don't have or don't want to hand-derive an analytic gradient/Hessian, and a `_closure` variant (v0.1.5) for when your objective needs to capture data by reference instead of being a plain top-level function pointer.

math_notes.sphere_fn: \( f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 = \lVert x \rVert^2 \) -- the simplest convex test objective, a single global minimum at the origin with circular (spherical) level sets, used throughout this package's own tests as the easy case every solver should converge on quickly.
math_notes.rosenbrock_fn: The Rosenbrock "banana" function \( f(x,y) = (1-x)^2 + 100(y-x^2)^2 \) (2-variable form) -- a classic hard test case: its minimum (at \( (1,1) \), value 0) sits inside a long, narrow, curved valley that plain gradient descent approaches very slowly even though the function itself is smooth and convex-ish near the minimum.
math_notes.rosenbrock_grad: The analytic gradient of `rosenbrock_fn`: \( \partial f/\partial x = -2(1-x) - 400x(y-x^2) \), \( \partial f/\partial y = 200(y-x^2) \).
math_notes.grad_fd: Approximates \( \nabla f(x) \) via central differences: \( \left(\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}\right)_i \approx \dfrac{f(x+he_i)-f(x-he_i)}{2h} \) for each standard basis vector \( e_i \) -- \( 2n \) evaluations of \( f \) for an \( n \)-dimensional gradient.
math_notes.hessian_fd: Approximates the Hessian matrix \( H_{ij} = \partial^2f/\partial x_i \partial x_j \) via a finite-difference second-derivative stencil in each pair of directions -- \( O(n^2) \) evaluations of \( f \), and (per the README) noticeably less accurate than an analytic Hessian (error roughly \( 10^{-6} \) to \( 10^{-4} \) depending on \( h \) and problem scale).
math_notes.gradient_descent_fixed: \( x_{k+1} = x_k - \alpha \nabla f(x_k) \) with a FIXED step size \( \alpha \) chosen by the caller -- the simplest possible descent method; converges only if \( \alpha \) is small enough for the problem's curvature, which this function does nothing to verify for you.
math_notes.armijo_line_search: Given a current point and a descent direction, finds a step size \( \alpha \) satisfying the Armijo (sufficient-decrease) condition \( f(x+\alpha d) \le f(x) + c_1 \alpha \nabla f(x)^T d \) via backtracking (halving \( \alpha \) starting from 1 until the condition holds) -- guarantees each accepted step actually makes meaningful progress, unlike a fixed step size that might overshoot or undershoot.
math_notes.gradient_descent_backtracking: Same update \( x_{k+1} = x_k - \alpha_k \nabla f(x_k) \) as `gradient_descent_fixed`, but \( \alpha_k \) is chosen fresh each iteration by `armijo_line_search` instead of being fixed -- adapts to the local curvature instead of requiring the caller to guess a single working step size in advance.
math_notes.newton_nd: Newton's method for minimization: \( x_{k+1} = x_k - H(x_k)^{-1}\nabla f(x_k) \), where \( H \) is the (caller-supplied, analytic) Hessian -- solved as a linear system \( H(x_k)\delta = -\nabla f(x_k) \) via `mat_solve` rather than explicitly inverting \( H \). Converges much faster than gradient descent near the minimum (quadratic vs. linear convergence rate) when \( H \) is available and positive-definite there.
math_notes.newton_nd_fd: Same Newton iteration as `newton_nd`, but the Hessian is approximated via `hessian_fd` instead of requiring an analytic one -- trades the accuracy/cost of an extra \( O(n^2) \) finite-difference evaluation per step for not needing a hand-derived second derivative.
math_notes.coordinate_descent: Minimizes one coordinate \( x_i \) at a time (cycling through \( i = 1, \ldots, n \) and back) while holding every other coordinate fixed, via a 1D line search along that single axis -- avoids needing a full gradient at all, at the cost of typically needing many more iterations than a method that uses gradient information from every dimension at once.
math_notes.quadratic_minimize: The exact closed-form minimizer of a convex quadratic \( f(x) = \tfrac{1}{2}x^TQx - b^Tx \): setting \( \nabla f(x) = Qx - b = 0 \) gives \( x^* = Q^{-1}b \), solved via `mat_solve` (not explicit inversion) -- valid only when \( Q \) is symmetric positive-definite, in which case this is the exact answer in one linear solve, not an iterative approximation.
math_notes.penalty_value: \( f(x) + \mu \sum_j \max(0, g_j(x))^2 \) -- the penalty-method objective: the original objective \( f \) plus a quadratic penalty term that grows only when a constraint \( g_j(x) \le 0 \) is VIOLATED (the \( \max(0,\cdot) \) means satisfied constraints contribute nothing), scaled by a penalty weight \( \mu \).
math_notes.penalty_method_minimize: Solves a constrained problem by minimizing `penalty_value`'s combined objective with an UNCONSTRAINED solver, then increasing the penalty weight \( \mu \) and re-minimizing from the previous solution, repeating -- as \( \mu \to \infty \) the penalty term forces the solution arbitrarily close to the feasible region, at the cost of the combined objective becoming increasingly ill-conditioned for large \( \mu \) (the classic penalty-method tradeoff).
math_notes.simplex_solve: The simplex method for linear programming: maximize \( c^Tx \) subject to \( Ax \le b,\ x \ge 0 \), by walking along the edges of the feasible polytope's vertices (each a basic feasible solution) via pivoting, always improving the objective, until no further improving pivot exists -- the exact (not approximate) LP solution, when one exists.
math_notes.simplex_value: \( c^Tx = \sum_i c_i x_i \) -- evaluates the linear objective at a given point, typically the solution `simplex_solve` returns.
